clue.text: Blonde with a Yankee, not rough

parts.note: blonde hair is fair hair
Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A fair-haired person arrives with an American, and the company is anything but rough.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf the rough is the long grass; the part of the course that is 'not rough' is the closely mown strip between tee and green.
explanation.definitionFit: On a golf course the mown playing strip is contrasted with the rough grass bordering it.

clue.text: Sporty type allowed to spike articles

indicators.note: to spike something is to pierce it, so one word is driven into the others

parts.note: a and the are the two English articles, indefinite and definite
let means allowed

explanation.surface: A sporty person was permitted to spike newspaper articles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spike' suggests killing a story or running spikes; here LET pierces A + THE.
explanation.definitionFit: An athlete is a sportsperson, especially one competing in track and field.

clue.text: Upset boozer? It's what nursery workers do

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the word is reversed

parts.note: a toper is a heavy drinker, a boozer

explanation.surface: An upset drunkard at a children's nursery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boozer' in British slang is also a pub, but here it is a drinker; 'nursery' means a plant nursery, not a creche.
explanation.definitionFit: Garden-centre staff move plants into new, larger pots as they grow.

clue.text: Dilettante couple enter a university run

indicators.note: the couple word goes into the pair of letters around it

parts.note: to mate is to couple or pair up
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A dabbling couple sign up to run a university.
explanation.definitionFit: A dilettante dabbles without professional skill, like someone doing a thing for love, not pay.

clue.text: Best expenses cover parking

indicators.note: the expenses word covers, or wraps around, the parking letter

parts.note: an outlay is money spent, expenses

explanation.surface: A query about whether expenses are best used to cover parking charges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best' is a verb here, to beat someone, not the adjective it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: To best an opponent is to beat them, which is to play better than them in a game.

clue.text: College that in Paris is without a match

parts.note: uni is short for university, a college
que is French for that

explanation.surface: A college in Paris that has no rival.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unique is one of a kind, with no equal or counterpart.

clue.text: Star to write quotation on pack

parts.note: to pen is to write
a tag is a well-known quotation or saying
to ram is to pack or cram tightly

explanation.surface: A celebrity writes a quote on a parcel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' suggests a celebrity, but it is the five-pointed figure.
explanation.definitionFit: A pentagram is a five-pointed star drawn with five straight lines.

clue.text: Plug smooth lecture

parts.note: a plug is a piece of advertising, an ad
to dress stone or timber is to smooth its surface

explanation.surface: A slick talk that is really a promotional plug.
explanation.definitionFit: An address is a formal speech given to an audience, much like a lecture.

clue.text: Kate's dithered in depicting sport

indicators.note: the jumbled name sits in the depicting word

parts.note: figuring is depicting, representing in a figure

indicators.note: dithered means agitated or confused, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Kate hesitated while drawing a sporting scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dithered' is the anagram signal, and 'in' tells you the jumbled name goes inside the depicting word rather than beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Figure skating is an Olympic ice sport of jumps, spins and set patterns.

clue.text: American's crisp approach to green

definitions.meaning: what Britons call a crisp, a thin fried potato slice
in golf a ... is a short lofted shot played onto the green

explanation.surface: A snack and a golf shot.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: the US word for a potato crisp, and a short golf stroke onto the putting surface.

clue.text: A timeless fable by a party devotee

indicators.note: time is abbreviated T, so without time the word loses that letter

parts.note: a fable is a work of fiction
a do is a party or social event

explanation.surface: A fable without any time setting is written by a devotee of parties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'timeless' removes T (time) from FICTION, leaving FICION.
explanation.definitionFit: An aficionado is an enthusiast, a keen follower of some pursuit.

clue.text: Recent changes back at Twickenham

indicators.note: the letters of the word undergo changes, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Recent personnel changes in the backs at England's rugby stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: Twickenham is England's national rugby stadium in London; in rugby union the centres are among the backs.
explanation.definitionFit: A centre is one of the rugby positions in the back line, alongside wings and full-back.

clue.text: A Scottish singer, laid back, oddly trendy, wailed

indicators.note: something laid back is turned backwards, so these letters are read in reverse

parts.note: Lulu is a Scottish pop singer

indicators.note: oddly signals taking the odd-numbered letters of the following word

explanation.surface: A relaxed, oddly fashionable Scottish singer let out a wail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laid back' reverses A plus LULU to give ULULA; 'oddly' takes the 1st, 3rd and 5th letters of trendy, TED.
explanation.definitionFit: To ululate is to howl or wail, a long rising cry of grief or celebration.

clue.text: Wool supplier hiding blemish books clothing course

indicators.note: the books letters wrap round, or clothe, everything else

parts.note: NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

indicators.note: the wool supplier conceals the blemish word inside it

parts.note: a ewe is a sheep, a supplier of wool
a mark is a blemish or spot

explanation.surface: A wool supplier hides a flaw while books cover the course material.
explanation.walkthrough: Two nested insertions: 'hiding' and 'clothing'. 'Course' is a racecourse: Newmarket is a famous English horse-racing town in Suffolk.
explanation.definitionFit: Newmarket is a racecourse, so 'course' is the racing sense of the word.

clue.text: Wealth check signifies big game

parts.note: means is signifies
a Test is a full international cricket or rugby match

explanation.surface: Checking someone's wealth signals a big-game hunt.
explanation.walkthrough: A means test is a British assessment of income that decides who gets state benefits.
explanation.definitionFit: A means test examines a person's income and savings to decide eligibility for help.

clue.text: Hibernian flag on hotel

parts.note: the yellow flag is a kind of iris, a wild flower
Hotel is H in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A national flag flying above a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flag' suggests a banner, but it is the plant name for an iris. Hibernia is the Latin name for Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Hibernian is a literary adjective for things from Ireland, from its Latin name.

clue.text: Race swimmer the Spanish introduced

indicators.note: the Spanish article is introduced into the swimmer word

parts.note: a ray is a flat fish, a swimmer
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: A swimming race into which the Spanish team was brought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swimmer' looks like a competitor, but it is a fish, the ray.
explanation.definitionFit: A relay is a team race in which each member runs or swims one leg in turn.

clue.text: Quartet aboard eastern vessel's hard to catch

indicators.note: the quartet number is put aboard, inside, the vessel

parts.note: a vase is a vessel
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A band of four aboard a ship from the east proves elusive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessel' suggests a ship but is a vase; the 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone evasive dodges questions or pursuit, so is slippery and elusive.

clue.text: Munro snubs a top high-flyer in the Alps?

indicators.note: to snub is to ignore, so the letter is left out of the writer's pen-name

parts.note: Saki was the pen-name of the writer H H Munro
a jumper is a knitted top, a sweater

explanation.surface: A Scottish mountain looking down on a lesser summit, beside a high flyer in the Alps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Munro' suggests a Scottish peak, but it is the writer H H Munro, known as Saki; dropping A gives SKI.
explanation.definitionFit: A ski jumper launches from a ramp and flies through the air, often in Alpine venues.

clue.text: Launching event broadcast live during month

indicators.note: the jumbled word falls during, inside, the month

parts.note: Jan is short for January

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A launch event broadcast live in a certain month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast live' reads as television coverage, but 'broadcast' is the anagram signal for live, and 'during' places the result inside the month.
explanation.definitionFit: The javelin is a field event in which a spear is thrown, or launched.

clue.text: Online topic for debate generating strong feeling?

parts.note: E as in e-mail stands for electronic, online
a motion is the proposition put up for debate

explanation.surface: An internet debate topic that stirs strong feelings.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotion is an intense feeling such as anger or joy.

clue.text: Order student what she claims to possess?

definitions.meaning: a trainee member of a religious order
a nun might claim to have ...

explanation.surface: A trainee nun claiming to be without sin.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer as NO VICE; 'she' is the novice herself.
explanation.definitionFit: A novice is a probationer who has entered a religious order but not taken final vows.

clue.text: Permit what posh diners do after meal?

definitions.text: what posh diners do after meal?
definitions.meaning: at formal dinners the port decanter is passed round the table

explanation.surface: A permit, and a dining ritual of the upper classes.
explanation.walkthrough: At formal British dinners the decanter of port is passed to the left after the meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A passport is an official travel document that permits entry, hence a permit in broad terms.

clue.text: What succeeds uniform winner

definitions.meaning: in the NATO phonetic alphabet ... follows Uniform

explanation.surface: What follows a uniform, and a winner.
explanation.definitionFit: Victor is the code word for V, which follows U in the alphabet; a victor is the one who wins.

clue.text: Stroke stomach close to navel

parts.note: a craw is the crop or stomach of a bird or animal

indicators.note: close means end, so close to takes the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Stroking the stomach close to the belly button.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stroke' suggests a caress; it is the swimming stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: The crawl is the fast front swimming stroke, also called freestyle.

clue.text: I'm stealing nuts and pips for one

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to stealing nuts and fruit stones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nuts and pips' look like snacks and seeds; 'nuts' is the anagram signal. The pips are the BBC radio's hourly time signal, six short beeps.
explanation.definitionFit: The radio pips are one example of a broadcast marking the exact time.

clue.text: Settled boxer beginning to tire

parts.note: Muhammad Ali was a famous boxer

indicators.note: beginning to signals the first letter of the next word

explanation.surface: The boxer settled the fight as his opponent began to tire.
explanation.definitionFit: Alit is a past tense of alight, so it means settled or landed, as a bird does.

clue.text: Hide article penned by humorous writer

indicators.note: the article is enclosed, or penned in, by the writer's name

parts.note: Edward Lear wrote comic nonsense verse
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A writer of comic verse hides a newspaper article he wrote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' looks like a verb, but it is the noun, an animal's skin; 'penned' plays on writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Leather is tanned animal skin, and a hide is the skin of a large animal.

clue.text: Mark avoids ruining Bankside pursuit

indicators.note: the word avoids, so goes without, the mark letter

parts.note: mangling is ruining or wrecking
M is short for mark, the old German currency

explanation.surface: Mark manages not to wreck a pastime on the riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' reads as a man's name, but it is M; 'Bankside' suggests London's South Bank, but means a riverbank.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglers fish from the banks of rivers, so angling is a riverside pastime.
